Here's the piece. I've kept it plain and put the practical details (fortnightly commitment, two-hour induction, paid-for food hygiene course, open afternoon) near the top so nobody has to hunt for them. I've left the volunteering line number as a placeholder.

---

**The Thursday tea trolley (or, how I lost a jug of milk)**

If you read this blog and assume that volunteering at a hospice must be either harrowing or something you need to be trained for, I would like to correct both assumptions.

I am 74. I retired from 41 years of bookkeeping, mostly for a builders' merchant in Dereham, and I started at Wensum Vale eighteen months later, in March 2022. That gap was not a plan. After retiring I had no regular reason to go out most weeks and I drifted a bit for a year and a half. Thursdays fixed that.

**What the job actually is.** I serve tea, coffee and biscuits on the trolley in the day therapy unit, Thursdays 1.30 to 4pm. On a typical Thursday the unit sees 14 to 18 patients. Many come for the art group or the hand massage, or just for the company. Most go home afterwards, which is as it should be.

**Time commitment.** One Thursday a fortnight. That is a real commitment and I won't pretend otherwise — when people fall ill or move away, the rest of us feel it. The rota is written for six of us. There are currently four. One of our number moved to Sheffield to be near her grandchildren; the other had a knee operation. We are two short, and Bridget would like to put that right.

**Induction.** Bridget does it, about two hours, and there is a short food hygiene course to do online, which the hospice pays for. You need no previous experience of anything.

**Some weeks are hard.** Patients are sometimes very unwell, and sometimes people die, and there are tears. That happens. The staff look after us when it does, and they are good at it. But I want to be accurate about the general run of it: it is not a sad place on a Thursday. It is noisy and rather jolly.

Mr Hollis, a retired signalman, takes two sugars and tells me about the 1953 floods every week, with slightly different dates each time. I have stopped correcting him.

My first week I put a full jug of milk over the trolley. A patient called Pat laughed so much she had to be given a tissue, and said it was the best afternoon she'd had in a month. I have thought about that more often than you might expect. None of this needs nursing skill. You need to push a trolley, remember who takes what, and listen. Forty-one years of keeping ledgers straight turns out to be handy for remembering who takes what.

The bourbon biscuits always go first. We now hide a packet for the late group.

**If you fancy a go.** Come to the volunteer open afternoon on **Tuesday 24 November, 2pm, in the Willow Room.** Tea and biscuits, no obligation, nothing to sign on the spot. Or ring Bridget on the volunteering line and have a chat. I came for a two-hour induction and a jug of milk, and have been turning up ever since.

---

Two small suggestions for getting those two extra bodies through the door: put the 24 November date in the newsletter's opening line rather than only at the bottom, and ask Bridget whether she'd be willing to ring one or two people she knows personally — a mention by name from a member of staff tends to work better than a blog post. A direct phone call to the volunteering line is probably the stronger of the two routes, so I would put both in the piece and the number at the top of your contacts list rather than buried in the footer.
